title: MA8-14268
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXXX, is a citizen of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. He is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
XXXXX XXXXX, from XXXXX, acted as the claimant's designated representative.

The claimant, who was a XXXXX and who apparently XXXXX XXXXX in Saint Vincent, experienced various acts of persecution because he criticized the authorities in place and because he practised Rastafarianism. The claimant also had difficulties stemming from his mental health problems.

The claimant arrived in Canada in XXXXX 2008. He consulted his lawyer, wrote up his story and filed his refugee protection claim. On October 28, 2008, his claim was referred to the Refugee Protection Division (RPD); however, the claimant did not contact his lawyer, and his Personal Information Form (PIF) was never completed and submitted.

On January 30, 2009, the RPD concluded that the claimant had abandoned his claim. On April 21, 2010, an application to reopen was allowed because of the claimant's mental health problems and because of allegations that he had been hospitalized on the day of the hearing on the abandonment of his claim.
After analyzing all of the evidence, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection." ANALYSIS Identity

The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity, which was demonstrated by the presence in the file of a copy of his passport, in the name of XXXXX XXXXX,1 and a certificate of a change of name from XXXXX XXXXX to XXXXX XXXXX.2 Procedural accommodations

The claimant allegedly suffers from some mental health problems. There is no official diagnosis for the problems, because he refuses to undergo treatment for them. The claimant, who is in detention at the Immigration Prevention Centre, was to consult a physician, in October 2010, for a psychiatric assessment; however, the claimant refused to undergo such an assessment.

The claimant's lawyer, some people who worked with him during his detention at the Immigration Prevention Centre,3 his designated representative, his sister, who testified at the hearing, and the panel before whom he testified, all noted that his statements were often incoherent. The claimant's designated representative described his behaviour as [translation] "erratic," which is consistent with what the panel observed in the hearing room. The claimant's lawyer also indicated the he had difficulty cooperating with her.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimant is unable to fully appreciate the nature of the proceedings, which is why a representative was designated for him under subsection 167(2) of the IRPA. Although no application was filed to have the claimant declared a vulnerable person, the panel ensured that, during the hearing, the necessary procedural accommodations were made to make it easier for the claimant to testify and present the elements in support of his claim.4
For example, the claimant was invited to speak about his claim, but the panel respected his wish to not be in the room during his sister's testimony and during his lawyer's statements.

The panel also allowed the claimant's lawyer to ask the questions first and allowed his designated representative to intervene when he thought it appropriate. Because of the claimant's defiance toward his lawyer, the tribunal officer and the panel both tried, in turn, to clarify certain points.

In addition, the panel scheduled a meeting after the hearing to find out about the XXXXX that the claimant had apparently XXXXX and that could not be filed at the hearing. During that meeting, which took place five days after the hearing, the claimant's lawyer informed the panel that the claimant's sister had found some supplementary documents in a suitcase he had left at her home. The panel allowed those documents to be filed, on the grounds of their relevance.5 The panel also granted an additional delay so that some documentary evidence could be filed on the situation of Rastafarians in the Caribbean and on the treatment of people with mental illness. Analysis of the claim under section 96 of the IRPA

Basically, it is alleged that the claimant was a XXXXX in his country and that he was persecuted by the authorities for his controversial opinions, which he allegedly expressed about the government. Also, the claimant converted to Rastafarianism, which apparently prompted him, in 1995, to change his name to one that more clearly expressed his faith and which allegedly became a new reason for his persecution. That alleged persecution supposedly had a negative effect on the claimant's mental health, which only served to aggravate his already difficult situation.

The claimant described his difficulties, at question 31 of his PIF. He stated that he was fired from his job in 1992, was evicted from several apartments, had trouble finding other jobs, XXXXX that the Saint Vincent government allegedly XXXXX XXXXX and was beaten up by some people who supported the government in 1996. In addition, the claimant's passport was allegedly revoked. He also claimed to have been poisoned every year until 2003. He also claimed that XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX had been stolen and that he had tried to start up a XXXXX XXXXX, but that initiative failed in 2002, when three of the investors apparently pulled out. On a number of occasions, people allegedly tried to discredit the claimant's work, the police supposedly dropped their investigation into the XXXXX theft and the claimant allegedly managed to obtain a passport after surviving an attempted murder that allegedly forced him to live on the street.

At the hearing, the claimant stated that what he had declared in his refugee protection claim was no longer valid. He stated that he agreed with the fact that he was going to be deported. He reiterated that what he feared two years earlier no longer existed and that what he had criticized the government for was [translation] "ancient history." When questioned again about what he had gone through in Saint Vincent, the claimant stated that it had happened in 2008, that it was a long time ago, and that he no longer wanted to obtain refugee status. When asked, [translation] "What would happen to you if you had to return to Saint Vincent?", the claimant replied that nothing in particular would happen to him. He stated that he would not have any problems if he had to return and that the truth must XXXXX XXXXX.

Since the claimant had nothing else to add, the panel let him leave the room. His lawyer and his designated representative then alleged that the claimant did not really understand the purpose of the proceedings and that he may have confused his refugee protection hearing with a detention review hearing. Since the claimant's main focus is on getting out of detention, he might have minimized what would happen to him in the hope of being released.

Given that information, the panel suggested that the designated representative meet privately with the claimant to explain to him once again the purpose of this hearing, and that the claimant could return and speak to the panel if he felt it necessary. The designated representative returned to the hearing room and reported that the claimant had stated that he had nothing to add.

The claimant's sister, XXXXX XXXXX, testified. She stated that her older brother had been a father figure to her. She stated that she has always had tremendous admiration for her brother, an erudite man who had worked hard to get an education, who had been a XXXXX and who had worked for the XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant's sister stated that she had left Saint Vincent in 1997 and that she did not know the claimant when he was sick. She apparently went back to Saint Vincent to visit in 2000, but allegedly did not see her brother then.

The claimant's sister allegedly received some calls from the family informing her that her brother was having problems. She was apparently told that her brother had been fired from his XXXXX when he expressed his beliefs in Rastafarianism, that some XXXXX and XXXXX had been stolen from him, that he had been beaten up often, and that acid had been thrown in his face, which led to his being hospitalized.

Ms. XXXXX apparently knew in 2008 that her older brother was suffering from mental health problems. A cousin who was working at a XXXXX where the claimant was staying allegedly contacted her to tell her that he was not well. Some family members allegedly asked Ms. XXXXX to arrange to get him out of the country.

According to the information that Ms. XXXXX had, her brother had been on medication when he was living in Saint Vincent. When he arrived in Canada, the effect of the medication, which he most likely stopped taking, gradually diminished and his condition seemed to worsen.

Ms. XXXXX stated that she believed that her brother had been persecuted for criticizing the government and that he had been ostracized for being Rastafarian. She stated that there is a great deal of discrimination against Rastafarians in Saint Vincent, that it is difficult for someone who wears a typically Rastafarian hairstyle to get a job and that it is quite possible that the police would cut her brother's hair if he were to be institutionalized again. She stated that the claimant risked being beaten again if he returned to his country and that she thought that his mental health problems stemmed from abuse he has suffered.

This is a complex situation, and all of the people involved have the best intentions. However, while the panel understands the difficulties associated with mental illness, the panel cannot, on the basis of the evidence at its disposal, conclude that there is a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if he had to return to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

The panel is willing to believe that the claimant is telling the truth when he states that he was a XXXXX in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. He has documents corroborating his claims in that regard.6 The panel also believes that the claimant is Rastafarian and that he has XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX,7 an intrinsic component of his faith. The panel is even prepared to give the claimant the benefit of the doubt that he XXXXX XXXXX that were critical of the Saint Vincent authorities and of the "establishment."

However, the panel does not have enough evidence to conclude that the claimant was a victim of persecution when he was living in Saint Vincent. In that regard, the panel has only vague information from the claimant's statements at question 31 of his PIF, who is likely mentally ill and who denied having problems at the hearing, and from his sister, who was not in Saint Vincent when these events allegedly occurred and who apparently obtained this information from another family member, without providing more details. The panel does not know who allegedly attacked the claimant, what the circumstances were surrounding the alleged attacks and what the apparent cause of it was.

According to the documentary evidence, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is a parliamentary democracy where there is freedom of expression and XXXXX XXXXX. The documentary evidence also indicates that the government generally respects these rights in practice.8 "XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX."

With regard to the fact that the claimant is Rastafarian, according to a document from 1993, people who practise Rastafarianism do sometimes face discrimination by the police and by the judicial system. For example, the police apparently perform illegal searches of Rastafarians and use violence against them during interrogations or detentions. It is also reportedly difficult for Rastafarians to find a job.9

Another, more recent, source, however, reported as follows: "With regard to discrimination faced by Rastafarians, the coordinator of the Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Human Rights Association (SVGHRA) based in Kingstown stated in a 28 October 2004 telephone interview that her organization had not received any complaints from Rastafarians who faced discrimination in connection with housing, education or employment. However, the coordinator did mention that she was aware of some harassment of Rastafarians by the police for marijuana use and cultivation, which, considering the country's laws, "would be expected10."
Similar information appears in a third documentary source: "Rastafarians complained that the government prohibited the use of marijuana, which they claimed was integral to their religious rituals11."

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees' Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status states that not all discrimination is necessarily persecution: "(c) Discrimination 54. Differences in the treatment of various groups do indeed exist to a greater or lesser extent in many societies. Persons who receive less favourable treatment as a result of such differences are not necessarily victims of persecution. It is only in certain circumstances that discrimination will amount to persecution. This would be so if measures of discrimination lead to consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature for the person concerned, e.g. serious restrictions on his right to earn his livelihood, his right to practise his religion, or his access to normally available educational facilities. 55. Where measures of discrimination are, in themselves, not of a serious character, they may nevertheless give rise to a reasonable fear of persecution if they produce, in the mind of the person concerned, a feeling of apprehension and insecurity as regards his future existence. Whether or not such measures of discrimination in themselves amount to persecution must be determined in the light of all the circumstances. A claim to fear of persecution will of course be stronger where a person has been the victim of a number of discriminatory measures of this type and where there is thus a cumulative element involved."

In light of that, and in the absence of additional information about what happened to the claimant-incidents that, at the hearing, the claimant denied ever happened-the panel cannot conclude that there is a serious possibility that the claimant will be persecuted for making comments critical of the government or the "establishment," or because he was Rastafarian.

In terms of his mental health problems, the panel cannot conclude that, in and of themselves, or combined with the claimant's religion, they constitute grounds for granting him refugee protection. The documentary evidence filed by the claimant's lawyer indicates that there is some prejudice with regard to mental illness in the Caribbean and that some taboos remain, but nothing indicates that people with mental illness are persecuted. "Too often, and especially in the Caribbean, ... we tend to view people with mental health illnesses as taboo, rather than recognizing that with treatment, recovery is possible. We also tend to forget that mental illness is not the result of personal weakness, but it can affect persons of any age, race, religion or income12."
In that regard, from the little the panel knows, the claimant received care and medication to improve his condition when he was in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

For the same reasons outlined above, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant is also not a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, since he did not demonstrate that he would be subjected to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment that do not result from his country's inability to provide proper medical or health care.

After analyzing all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant did not discharge the burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility that he was persecuted on one of the Convention grounds. He did not establish that, on a balance of probabilities, if he were to return to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
For all of those reasons, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection."

The panel rejects the refugee protection claim of XXXXX.
